results.summary: This design implements a two-player secret guessing game in which one player sets a 4-bit secret and the other has five rounds to guess it. Inputs set the secret, start the game, and submit guesses, while outputs report how many digits are correct in position and how many are correct but misplaced. It is a small state-machine design with no external hardware required beyond switches and LEDs for the inputs and outputs. The documentation is brief and contains typos, but the pin names and test steps are sufficient to understand the intended use.

This analog project is a seven-inverter ring oscillator intended to compare PEX simulation against measured silicon behavior. A chain of selectable dividers reduces the oscillator frequency by factors from 2 to 256, and the divided signal is routed to a digital output or, when enabled, to an analog pin through a buffer. Testing requires only setting the reset, enable, and select pins and observing the output, with no external hardware needed. The design is notable as a process and simulation-correlation experiment rather than a functional end product.

This chip is the control core for a capacitive-discharge model rocket launch controller, managing capacitor charging, igniter continuity testing, current-controlled igniter drive, and a safety energy dump. It uses three PWM outputs to drive a flyback charger, a buck igniter driver, and a dump FET, with feedback from an external three-channel ADC over a serial interface. A built-in self-test runs a truncated system simulation after reset and reports pass or fail through the output pins. The design requires substantial external hardware including ADCs, power FETs, a transformer, a speaker, buttons, and LEDs, and is notable for implementing a complete safety-critical control system on a tiny tile.

TinyFarm is a hardware farming game implemented in SystemVerilog that maintains four fields with crops that grow, can be watered, and are harvested to fulfill customer orders. Player inputs select mode, field, and crop and trigger actions, while a VGA output in RGB222 format displays the farm grid and game status. The design needs a Tiny VGA PMOD and a monitor to view the output, plus buttons or switches for the control inputs. It originated as a university final project and is notable for fitting a small game with inventory and order logic into a single tile pair.

This project is a complete 8-bit accumulator-based microcontroller SoC with a 33-instruction ISA, a 32-word program ROM, 32 bytes of RAM shared with a hardware stack, a UART transmitter, a timer, and 8-bit GPIO. It runs a hardcoded demo program that counts on the GPIO outputs, calls a subroutine, sends a character over UART, reads the timer, and then halts. Testing involves applying reset and enable, then observing the GPIO outputs and the UART TX pin, optionally with LEDs and a USB-UART adapter connected. The design is notable for packing a full CPU with memory, stack, and peripherals into a small two-tile area.

Flappy VGA is a simplified Flappy Bird-style game implemented entirely in digital logic, generating VGA timing and rendering a bird, moving pipes, ground, and background in real time. A physics module applies gravity and responds to a jump button, while collision detection ends the game when the bird hits a pipe or the ground. The design outputs 2-bit RGB with HSYNC and VSYNC and requires a Tiny VGA PMOD or resistor-DAC circuit plus a VGA monitor and two push buttons. It is notable for implementing a complete interactive game with sprite rendering and collision logic in a small tile area.

This analog test project is intended to measure punch-through current, with five analog pins exposed for connection to a multimeter. The documentation consists only of placeholder text and does not explain the structure, biasing, or expected measurements of the test structure. No external hardware beyond a multimeter is mentioned, and no test procedure is given. The available documentation is essentially empty, so the design cannot be described in detail.

This design implements a 16-bit Galois LFSR random number generator with user-selectable shift direction and 32 different feedback polynomials, including standard CRC-16 polynomials and experimental tap patterns. Inputs select enable, direction, and polynomial, and the 16-bit state is exposed on the output and bidirectional pins for observation on LEDs. Testing requires only DIP switches and LEDs, with no external hardware needed. The design is notable for exposing a wide range of standard and experimental polynomials for comparison and educational use.

This project implements a finite state machine that controls an automatic garage door opener, handling open, close, and stop commands from a single button plus position and obstruction sensors. Outputs drive an up motor and a down motor, and an obstruction input causes the door to stop and reverse while closing. Testing can be done with two LEDs on the motor outputs or with an H-bridge and DC motor, and the design is a straightforward educational FSM example. The documentation is clear but brief, and the design is small and self-contained.

This project implements a Direct Digital Synthesis waveform generator with a phase accumulator and a 16-entry lookup table, producing sine, sawtooth, square, triangle, and quadratic waveforms. Inputs select the waveform function, amplitude, and frequency control word, and an 8-bit digital output carries the generated samples. An external DAC and oscilloscope are required to view the analog waveform, and the design is notable for offering multiple waveform types and programmable frequency and amplitude in a single tile. The documentation is clear and includes the DDS frequency formula and test steps.
